title: Internal energy, specific heat capacity and latent heat

tips.title: Delta theta is a change
tips.body: $\Delta\theta$ is the **change** in temperature, not the final one. From 20 °C to 50 °C it is **30**. Writing 50 is the single most common error in the topic, and it makes every answer too big.

tips.title: Is the temperature changing?
tips.body: Temperature **changing** means $\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta$. Temperature **constant** while the state changes means $E = mL$. If a question spans both, do two calculations and **add** them: heat to the boiling point, then boil.

tips.title: Fusion melts, vaporisation boils
tips.body: **Fusion** is solid to liquid; **vaporisation** is liquid to gas. Vaporisation is far larger, about seven times for water, because the particles must be separated completely rather than merely loosened.

tips.title: Both equations are on the sheet
tips.body: $\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta$ and $E = mL$ are **given**, so do not waste revision memorising them. Spend it on choosing the right one and on the units: mass in **kilograms**, never grams.

why.matters:
Heating something does one of two things and never both at once: it makes the particles move faster, which you feel as **temperature**, or it pulls them apart, which you see as **melting or boiling**. Specific heat capacity and latent heat are the prices of each, per kilogram.

Once you know the two prices you can say how long the kettle takes, why steam scalds worse than boiling water, why the sea is cold in June, and why a change of state is where most of the energy goes.

examples.title: Hot sand, cold sea
examples.body:
At noon the sand burns your feet and the sea is still cold. Both have had the same sun on them all morning. Water's specific heat capacity is 4 200 J/kg°C; dry sand's is about 800. Warming a kilogram of water by 10 °C takes 42 000 J, and a kilogram of sand only 8 000 J, so the same energy lifts the sand's temperature more than five times as far.

After dark the sand is cold within an hour and the sea is still warm, because it has five times the energy to give back per degree. The sea is warmest in September, not June, for the same reason.

boxes.body: Too hot to stand on. About 8 000 J warms a kilogram by ten degrees.

boxes.body: Still cold. It takes 42 000 J to warm a kilogram by ten degrees.

boxes.title: Sand at midnight
boxes.body: Cold within an hour of sunset. Little energy stored, so little to give back.

examples.title: Why steam scalds worse than boiling water
examples.body:
Both are at 100 °C, so it is not the temperature. A gram of boiling water landing on skin cools from 100 °C to about 37 °C and gives up $4200 \times 0.001 \times 63$, about 265 J.

A gram of steam has to **condense** first. That releases its latent heat of vaporisation, $2 260 000 \times 0.001 = 2 260$ J, before it has cooled by a single degree, and then it cools as well. That is more than eight times the energy into the same patch of skin, which is why the burn from a kettle's spout is so much worse than a splash.

props.caption: Energy given to your skin by one gram of each, both starting at 100 °C.

visual.alt: Two bars drawn to scale comparing the two thousand two hundred and sixty joules a gram of steam releases as it condenses with the two hundred and sixty five a gram of boiling water gives up cooling to skin temperature

examples.title: Why ice cools a drink and cold water does not
examples.body:
An ice cube of 20 g at 0 °C and 20 g of water at 0 °C are the same temperature. In a drink they are not the same at all.

The water can only warm up. Taking it from 0 °C to 10 °C draws $4200 \times 0.02 \times 10$, 840 J, from the drink. The ice has to **melt** first, and melting 20 g draws $334 000 \times 0.02$, 6 680 J, from the drink without warming at all, and only then does its meltwater warm. Eight times the cooling from the same 20 g.

steps.title: Internal energy
steps.body:
The **internal energy** of a system is the **total kinetic energy and potential energy of all its particles**. Learn that sentence: it is a definition mark.

- The **kinetic** part is the movement of the particles, and it sets the **temperature**.
- The **potential** part is the energy stored in the forces between particles, and it sets the **state**.

Heating a system raises its internal energy, and that does one of exactly two things:

1. It **raises the temperature**, if the particles simply move faster.
2. It **changes the state**, if the particles are being pulled apart instead.

While a substance is melting or boiling it does one or the other, not both, which is why a temperature-time graph for melting ice has a flat section.

**Evaporation is the exception worth knowing.** Particles do not all move at the same speed, so even well below the boiling point the fastest ones at the surface can escape. That is why a pan of water at 60 °C warms and evaporates at the same time, and it is about the spread of speeds, not about the water being impure.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on internal energy: what it is, the kinetic part, the potential part, and the two things heating can do

check.solution: Internal energy is the **total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles** in the system. Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy, which is only part of it.

steps.title: Specific heat capacity
steps.body:
**Specific heat capacity** is the energy needed to raise the temperature of **1 kg** of a substance by **1 °C**. Water's is $4200$ J/kg°C, which is unusually high and is why it is used in heating systems.

$$\Delta E = m c \Delta\theta$$

The equation is **given on the equation sheet**, so the marks are in choosing it, substituting correctly and handling the units.

steps.title: Changing state, and why the temperature stops rising
steps.body:
While something is melting or boiling, the **temperature does not change**, even though energy is still going in. That flat section on a heating graph is the part exam questions are set on.

The reason is the split in internal energy. During a change of state the energy goes into the **potential** part, pulling the particles apart against the forces between them, not into the **kinetic** part. No change in kinetic energy means no change in temperature.

**Specific latent heat** is the energy needed to change the state of **1 kg** with **no change in temperature**.

$$E = m L$$

- **Specific latent heat of fusion**: solid to liquid, $334,000$ J/kg for water.
- **Specific latent heat of vaporisation**: liquid to gas, $2,260,000$ J/kg for water.

Vaporisation costs far more because the particles must be separated completely, not merely loosened.

steps.title: Reading heating and cooling graphs
steps.body:
You should be able to **interpret heating and cooling graphs that include changes of state**. Every such graph is made of two kinds of section, and naming them is most of the marks.

The graph below is for **0.50 kg of ice** at −20 °C heated by a **1000 W** heater, assuming every joule goes into the water. It has four sections:

- **A, sloping: the ice warms** from −20 °C to 0 °C.
- **B, flat at 0 °C: the ice melts.** Energy is still going in, but it goes into the **potential** part of the internal energy, so the temperature does not rise. The temperature of a flat section **is the melting point**.
- **C, sloping: the water warms** from 0 °C to 100 °C.
- **D, flat at 100 °C: the water boils.** The flat section is at the boiling point. At 1000 W it would last 1130 s, so the graph stops part-way through.

**Sloping sections are specific heat capacity; flat sections are specific latent heat.** That is the distinction the specification asks you to make. On a sloping section the temperature changes and $\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta$ applies. On a flat section it does not change and $E = mL$ applies.

**The lengths and slopes are information.** The heater supplies the same energy every second, so:

- **A longer flat section means a bigger latent heat.** Melting takes 167 s; boiling takes 1130 s, about 6.8 times as long, because the specific latent heat of vaporisation is about 6.8 times that of fusion.
- **A steeper slope means a smaller specific heat capacity.** Ice warms at about 0.95 °C per second and water at about 0.48 °C per second. Ice's specific heat capacity, 2100 J/kg°C, is half of water's.

**Reading a latent heat off the graph.** The melt lasts from 21 s to 188 s, which is 167 s. Energy supplied $= P \times t = 1000 \times 167 = 167{,}000$ J. Then $L = \dfrac{E}{m} = \dfrac{167{,}000}{0.50} = 334{,}000$ J/kg, which is the value for water.

**A cooling curve is the same picture run backwards.** A liquid cools, then the graph goes **flat while it freezes**, then the solid cools. The flat section is at the **freezing point**, which is the same temperature as the melting point. It stays flat because the particles **release energy** as the forces between them pull them together, and that balances what is lost to the surroundings.

**Cooling curves are curved.** Something hot loses energy faster than something barely warmer than the room, so the curve is steep at first and levels off. It never falls below room temperature. In the second graph, substance X freezes at 55 °C.

visuals.alt: A heating graph for 0.50 kg of ice heated at 1000 W. The temperature rises from minus 20 to 0 °C in 21 s, stays at 0 °C until 188 s while the ice melts, rises to 100 °C at 398 s, then stays at 100 °C while the water boils.
A cooling graph for substance X. The liquid cools from 90 °C, curving, to 55 °C, stays at 55 °C for 240 s while it freezes, then the solid cools, curving towards room temperature.

steps.title: Your turn: two stages, one answer
steps.body:
A kettle supplies energy at **2000 W** to **0.5 kg of water at 20 °C**.

1. How much energy raises it to 100 °C? Use $c = 4200$ J/kg°C.
2. How long does that take, using $E = Pt$?
3. How much more energy would boil it all away? Use $L = 2,260,000$ J/kg.
4. How long would **that** take?

Compare your two times before you write anything down. The ratio is the point of the question.

visuals.alt: A blank table for the two stages of heating and boiling half a kilogram of water, with columns for the energy and the time at two thousand watts

steps.title: Going deeper: why the experiment always overestimates
steps.body:
A specific heat capacity experiment measures the energy supplied, the mass and the temperature rise, then divides. The value it gives is almost always **too high**, and explaining why is the classic six-mark question.

**The reason.** Not all the energy supplied reaches the block. Some goes to the surroundings, some warms the container and the heater itself. So the $\Delta E$ used in the calculation is bigger than the energy that actually raised the block's temperature. Dividing too large an energy by the same $m\Delta\theta$ gives too large a $c$.

**The improvements**, each with its reason:

- **Insulate** the block, to cut the energy lost to the surroundings.
- **Start below room temperature and finish above it**, so heat gained early cancels heat lost late.
- **Stir**, so the thermometer reads the whole block rather than a hot spot.
- **Wait** after switching off, because the temperature keeps rising for a few seconds.
- **Repeat and take a mean**, though note this one is different: it reduces **random** error and does nothing about the systematic overestimate above.

Name an improvement without its reason and you lose the marks for the reasons.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Internal energy** is the **total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles**.
- Heating either **raises the temperature** or **changes the state**, never both at once.
- **Specific heat capacity** is the energy to raise **1 kg** by **1 °C**. $\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta$, given on the sheet.
- $\Delta\theta$ is a **change**: from 20 °C to 50 °C is 30, not 50.
- **Specific latent heat** is the energy to change the state of **1 kg** with **no temperature change**. $E = mL$, also given.
- **Fusion** is solid to liquid; **vaporisation** is liquid to gas, and costs far more.
- During a change of state the energy goes into the **potential** part of the internal energy, so the graph is flat.
- On a heating or cooling graph, **sloping** sections are specific heat capacity and **flat** sections are changes of state, at the melting or boiling point. A **longer flat** means a bigger latent heat.
- A question spanning both needs **two calculations added**: heat to the boiling point, then boil.
- The measured $c$ comes out **too high**, because energy supplied is lost to the surroundings.
- Water: $c = 4200$ J/kg°C, $L_f = 334,000$ J/kg, $L_v = 2,260,000$ J/kg.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Stage 1: heat it.** $\Delta\theta = 100 - 20 = 80$ °C.

$$\Delta E = 0.5 \times 4200 \times 80 = 168,000 \text{ J}$$

$$t = \dfrac{E}{P} = \dfrac{168,000}{2000} = \mathbf{84} \text{ s}$$

**Stage 2: boil it dry.** No temperature change, so use $E = mL$.

$$E = 0.5 \times 2\,260\,000 = 1,130,000 \text{ J}$$

$$t = \dfrac{1,130,000}{2000} = \mathbf{565} \text{ s}$$

Boiling takes about **6.7 times** as long as all that heating, which is why a kettle left on takes a long time to boil dry.

questions.prompt: A student measures the specific heat capacity of a metal block and gets a value higher than the true one. Explain why, and describe two improvements with a reason for each.
questions.solution: The specific heat capacity is worked out by dividing the energy supplied by the mass times the temperature rise. The energy supplied is measured at the heater, but not all of it reaches the block: some is transferred to the surroundings and some warms the container and the heater itself. The number on the top of the fraction is therefore larger than the energy that actually raised the block's temperature, while the mass and the temperature rise are measured correctly, so the calculated value comes out too high. One improvement is to insulate the block, which reduces the energy transferred to the surroundings and so brings the energy supplied closer to the energy received. Another is to wait a little after switching the heater off before taking the final temperature, because the temperature continues to rise for a few seconds as energy spreads through the block, and reading too early makes the temperature rise look smaller than it was.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why it is too high.** The student calculates

$$c = \dfrac{\Delta E}{m \Delta\theta}$$

using the energy **supplied** at the heater. Not all of that reaches the block: some is transferred to the surroundings, and some warms the container and the heater itself. The **numerator** is therefore larger than the energy that actually raised the block's temperature, while $m$ and $\Delta\theta$ are measured correctly. A larger top over the same bottom gives a **larger** $c$.

**Improvement 1: insulate the block.** This reduces the energy transferred to the surroundings, so the energy supplied is closer to the energy the block receives.

**Improvement 2: wait before the final reading.** The temperature keeps rising for a few seconds after the heater is switched off, as energy spreads through the block. Reading too early makes $\Delta\theta$ look smaller than it really was.

questions.solution: A flat section on a heating graph is a **change of state**. Energy is still going in, but it is pulling the particles apart, so the temperature stays at the **melting point**, 80 °C.

questions.prompt: On a heating graph, water boils at 100 °C for 1130 s while a 1000 W heater supplies energy. Calculate the energy supplied during boiling, in J.
questions.solution: $E = Pt = 1000 \times 1130 = $ **1,130,000 J**. That is the energy for the change of state, so it equals $mL_v$.

questions.prompt: Ice is heated at a steady rate. On the heating graph, the ice warms at about 1.0 °C per second and the water later warms at about 0.5 °C per second. What explains the difference?
questions.solution: The heater supplies the same energy each second. Ice has specific heat capacity 2100 J/kg°C and water 4200 J/kg°C, so each degree of ice needs **half** the energy and its temperature rises **twice as fast**. Latent heat belongs to the flat sections, not the slopes.

examTechnique.body:
Write the three quantities down before substituting: mass in kilograms, the capacity or latent heat, and the temperature change. Listing them catches a mass given in grams, which is the error that ruins most of these calculations.

Ask whether the temperature is changing. If it is, use $\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta$. If it is constant while the state changes, use $E = mL$. A question that spans both needs two calculations added together, and the marks are split between them.

Use the change in temperature, not the final temperature. From 20 °C to 100 °C is 80.

Both equations are given on the sheet, so the marks are for choosing correctly and substituting, not for recall. Show the substitution before the answer.

For an evaluation question, name the improvement **and** the error it reduces. Half the marks in a six-marker are for the reasons, not the list.

On a heating or cooling graph, name each section: **sloping** is a temperature change (specific heat capacity), **flat** is a change of state (latent heat), and the flat temperature is the melting or boiling point.
examinerErrors: Using the final temperature instead of the change, so 100 goes in where 80 belongs.
Leaving the mass in grams, making every answer a thousand times too large.
Using mcΔθ for a change of state, where there is no temperature change at all.
Using E = mL for a temperature change, where there is no state change.
Doing only one stage of a question that needs heating and then boiling.
Confusing fusion with vaporisation, and using the wrong latent heat.
Saying internal energy is the heat in a substance, rather than the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles.
Listing improvements to an experiment without saying what error each one reduces.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes the quantities out with units before substituting, and converts grams to kilograms without being reminded. It decides between the two equations by asking whether the temperature is changing, and when a question needs both it does the two stages separately and adds them, saying which is which. It defines internal energy as the total kinetic and potential energy of the particles, and explains a flat section on a heating graph by saying the energy goes into the potential part. Asked to evaluate the experiment, it explains that the energy supplied exceeds the energy received, so the calculated value is too high, and pairs every improvement with the specific error it reduces.
